extracted.intended_audience: scientists, policymakers and general readers interested in stem-cell research, research ethics and scientific misconduct
extracted.subtask_description: A chronological news timeline recounting events, investigations, legal actions and editorial decisions in the Woo Suk Hwang stem-cell research controversy; documents standards and failures in research ethics, publication integrity, and institutional response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data fabrication / research-data integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Significant amounts of data presented in a paper that are fabricated render the results invalid and justify retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science's editorial retraction: “Because the final report of the SNU investigation indicated that a significant amount of the data presented in both papers is fabricated, the editors of Science feel that an immediate and unconditional retraction of both papers is needed… the results reported in them are deemed to be invalid.” Example: SNU investigation found large amounts of fabricated data in the 2005 paper (two cell lines used instead of 11), leading to retraction. Anti-pattern: treating deliberate fabrication as a mere 'error'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship and co-author consent procedures for retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals may require the research team/co-authors to be engaged in the retraction process and may wait for co-author agreement before finalizing wording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science said it must wait for the entire research team to consent to the retraction and that finalizing the wording 'should take days or weeks - not months.' Example: Science delayed final retraction wording pending team consent; later issued editorial retraction when fabrication was confirmed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informed consent and non-coercion for human-egg donors
rubrics_metrics.description: Egg donors must give informed, voluntary consent and must be made aware of potential risks; coercion (e.g., soliciting eggs from junior lab members) is ethically problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IRB and reporting findings discussed whether junior lab members donated voluntarily; many donors later reported side effects and said they were not told of risks. The Helsinki Guidelines (1964) prohibit coercion of research subjects; donors must be informed about risks. Anti-pattern: recruiting donors from vulnerable or subordinate groups without transparent consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment for eggs and compliance with bioethics law
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jurisdictions outlaw purchasing eggs for research; paying donors can violate bioethics statutes and trigger legal action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hwang was charged with violating a bioethics law that outlaws the purchase of eggs for research. The timeline notes admissions of payments for eggs and subsequent legal and public fallout. Example: indictment for violating bioethics law; lawsuits by donors claiming they were not made aware of risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing criteria for embryonic stem-cell research
rubrics_metrics.description: Licenses to conduct certain types of stem-cell research may require demonstrated recent publication or other credentials; loss of those credentials can revoke licensing eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Korean licensing rule cited: having at least one publication in embryonic stem-cell science in the past three years was a legal requirement for a licence. Retraction of Hwang’s papers meant he no longer met this requirement and lost his licence to conduct embryonic stem-cell research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biological-material provenance and DNA-matching validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that cell lines derive from specific patients require DNA fingerprint matching between the lines and the stated patient tissues; mismatches raise concerns about contamination or fabrication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MBC sent samples to an independent lab and reported that DNA in one cell line did not match the tissue sample as it should. Possible explanations include contamination, but mismatches can indicate that lines were not patient-specific as claimed. Example: SNU investigators found many lines did not match patients; calls for independent validation and replication followed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image and supporting-material integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Duplication or inappropriate manipulation of images and supporting materials undermines trust and must be corrected; even if not affecting main conclusions, such errors indicate quality-control failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hwang alerted Science to redundant images in Supporting Online Material; Science determined redundant images were inserted later and said the mistake did not affect the paper's scientific conclusions. Nonetheless, image duplication prompted scrutiny and corrections. Anti-pattern: leaving duplicated or manipulated images unaddressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper attribution and honest description of contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should accurately report their level of involvement and credit; overstating contribution or taking undue credit is misconduct-adjacent and undermines collaboration trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gerald Schatten was 'chided for taking so much credit for research in which he was barely involved.' Co-authors asked for retraction when new information cast substantial doubts on accuracy. Guidance: authors should disclose true roles and investigate concerns promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial integrity: misuse of funds and funding-related fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Using fabricated data to obtain research funding or embezzling funds constitutes legal and ethical violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hwang was indicted on charges including embezzling KRW2.8 billion and committing fraud by knowingly using fabricated data to apply for research funds. Example: prosecutors investigated misuse of state funds and fraud in funding applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional investigation standards and public reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Universities and IRBs must investigate allegations, assess whether issues are errors or deliberate fabrication, and report findings; their determinations guide journal and legal actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seoul National University carried out a rapid investigation, presented televised findings declaring deliberate fabrication for the 2005 paper, and the university committee delivered a verdict that the 2004 and 2005 papers were based on fraudulent data. IRBs also examined consent/payment issues and issued findings about voluntariness and payments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent replication and community validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Extraordinary claims should be validated by independent groups; the scientific community may call for independent tests of key materials or results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A letter from eight scientists (including Ian Wilmut) in Science encouraged Hwang's laboratory to cooperate to perform independent tests of his cell lines. Nature and others reported calls for independent validation after concerns arose. Example: scientists urged cooperation for independent testing of cell lines to resolve doubts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media-investigation ethics and accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigative reporting into scientific claims must adhere to accuracy and fair methods; broadcasters may need to apologize or correct inaccurate or problematic tactics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Munhwa Broadcasting Corporation (MBC) aired an investigative programme that later apologized for some reporting tactics. Media investigations can reveal problems (e.g., DNA tests) but must maintain ethical standards; flawed tactics can undermine credibility and lead to retractions/apologies.
